analysis.one_liner: Raises pay, safety, and anti-retaliation protections for meatpacking and food workers who supply USDA contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a Senate committee without a hearing, markup, or vote, after attracting three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have used the government's buying power to lift pay for food and meatpacking workers: the Agriculture Department could not buy from plants paying below the local prevailing wage, companies getting USDA contracts could not spend that period buying back their own stock, and repeated violators of labor laws could be barred from USDA contracts. It would also cap line speeds in meat and poultry plants, require OSHA to write ergonomic and bathroom-access rules for those plants, fund more federal safety inspectors, and make it easier for workers to sue over unsafe conditions or retaliation. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2023 and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Meatpacking and poultry workers — a heavily immigrant, low-wage workforce with injury rates well above the private-sector average — would gain higher pay floors on USDA purchases, slower line speeds, enforced bathroom-break rights, new ergonomic protections, $60 million a year for more federal safety inspectors, and stronger tools to sue employers who retaliate for reporting injuries or unsafe conditions. Companies that comply with labor laws would compete on a level field against violators.

how_it_helps.text: USDA could not buy meat, poultry, or processed food produced by workers paid below the local prevailing wage and benefits rate, as determined by the Labor Department [S2].
Companies holding USDA contracts would be barred from buying back their own stock or paying shareholder dividends during the contract period [S2].

Contractors would have to disclose labor-law violations, and repeat or serious violators would be placed on a list making them ineligible for USDA contracts — and ineligible for federal meat inspection — for five years [S2].
USDA could not issue waivers or policies that raise slaughter line speeds unless safety officials certified worker safety would not suffer, and no funds could be used to increase line speeds [S2].

OSSHA would have to write standards for ergonomics and for prompt medical referrals at meat and poultry plants, verify bathroom access and paid restroom breaks during inspections, and run permanent regional inspection programs covering amputation, line-speed, and chemical hazards [S2].
The bill appropriates $60 million a year for fiscal years 2024 through 2029 to hire additional OSHA inspectors [S2].

Meat and poultry workers would get a private right to sue over unsafe conditions or retaliation, with an expedited complaint process, a presumption of retaliation when adverse action follows protected activity within 90 days, and protection against being reported to immigration authorities for raising safety concerns [S2].

Employers would no longer be able to use no-fault point systems that punish workers for taking legally protected leave without clear written notice and a process to contest wrongly assessed points [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large meat and poultry processors and other food companies that sell to USDA would bear the cost: paying prevailing wages, forgoing stock buybacks and dividends during contract periods, disclosing violations and risking five-year debarment, slowing or holding line speeds, and facing new OSHA standards, inspections, and lawsuits. Domestic school-food suppliers would benefit from tighter restrictions on foreign purchases, while schools could face limits on buying cheaper foreign products.

drawbacks.text: The buyback and dividend ban applies only while a company holds USDA business, so it protects taxpayer money but does not stop the same companies from returning cash to shareholders from other revenue; and the extra strings could discourage firms from bidding on USDA contracts at all [S2].

The prevailing-wage rule, violation-disclosure system, and debarment list add significant compliance and administrative work for USDA, the Labor Department, and contractors, and the five-year inspection prohibition for listed plants is a powerful penalty whose accuracy would depend on the disclosure system working correctly [S2].

Tightening the school-lunch buy-American rules could raise costs or reduce choices for school food authorities, which is why the bill requires a waiver only when domestic goods are unavailable, inadequate, or significantly more expensive [S2].

Stronger retaliation rules, a private right of action, and expanded inspection programs would increase litigation and enforcement costs in an industry that argues its margins are thin — a cost that could partly pass through to prices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a well-documented problem: meat and poultry processing is among the most dangerous low-wage work in the country, and the bill's own findings cite double the private-industry amputation rate and musculoskeletal injuries exceeding 50 percent of workers [S2]. The costs fall almost entirely on large processors and on government administrative capacity, not directly on consumers, though prices and contract participation could shift. The main design criticism is that some remedies — the buyback ban and the debarment-with-inspection-stop provision — are blunt instruments that could discourage contractors or misfire, but the core worker-safety provisions track standard occupational-health practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2023 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the Agricultural Worker Justice Act on July 27, 2023, with Senators Booker and Wyden as original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action [S4].
The cosponsor page lists three Democratic cosponsors, out of 48 Senate Democrats, and no Republican support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processors and other USDA food contractors are better off: no prevailing-wage requirement on federal food purchases, no buyback ban, no violation disclosures or debarment risk, no line-speed limits, and no new OSHA ergonomics standards or expanded inspections.

sides.party_line_note: All three cosponsors were Democrats (3 of 48 Senate Democrats), no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond referral in the Democratic-led committee [S3][S4].

industries.note: The industry's plants would face prevailing-wage requirements on USDA purchases, a buyback and dividend ban while holding USDA contracts, line-speed limits, new OSHA ergonomics and medical-referral standards, more inspections, and worker lawsuits with a retaliation presumption. The industry's interest in keeping fast lines, low pay, and weak enforcement runs against the workers' interest in safety and wages [S2].

industries.industry: USDA food contractors and processed food companies
industries.note: Contractors would have to disclose violations of 21 labor laws or face a five-year ban on USDA contracts, plus a criminal penalty for knowingly failing to disclose. Their interest in avoiding disclosure and debarment runs against the public interest in holding federally funded employers to labor standards [S2].
The bill authorizes $400 million a year for the local food purchase assistance program, which channels USDA money to local and regional producers and the communities they supply [S2].

Tighter buy-American rules would require schools to seek a waiver before buying foreign food products, steering purchases toward domestic producers. This protects domestic jobs but can limit schools' ability to buy cheaper imports, potentially raising school food costs [S2].
